name: Aaron Larsen

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for joining me. I'm from the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group. We're not connected to AI companies, employers, unions or government, and everything you say is confidential. What does a normal working day look like for you?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm at Kestrel Autos, a garage on the industrial estate that does a lot of hybrids and imported Japanese cars. First thing I run the overnight fault logs through an AI assistant on my phone so I've got a shortlist before the customer even arrives. Then it's hands in: inverter coolant, brake jobs, battery checks, the odd timing chain. I love the puzzle of a weird hybrid fault, and I hate how little the job pays for how much you have to know now.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: How did you end up using AI so much?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I got sick of waiting for the old diagnostic database to load, so I started asking a chatbot and checking its answers against the manuals. Now Priyesh, the owner, asks me to look things up for the others. I'm the one who's quick with it, though I'm still on lower pay than the guy at the main dealer across town.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Bit of a letdown, honestly. I'd half hoped it would get properly good.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say the tools are handy but they're not magic, and anyone who said otherwise was selling something. At work I'd keep using the assistant for wiring diagrams. Online I'd probably post a few of the dumb answers it gave me for a laugh.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, it means my edge is smaller. Being the AI guy at Kestrel is part of why Priyesh values me. If AI stays a bit useful and nothing more, I'm just an average mechanic on below-average pay with three weeks of rent in the bank.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep using it every day, because it still saves me twenty minutes a job. I'd push Priyesh for a raise on the back of the hybrid work. And I'd try to save, maybe by selling the motorbike I never ride.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A bit flat. Not scared, just stuck. Sam, my partner, keeps saying we should think about moving somewhere cheaper.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you move?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Maybe, but there are only two garages within half an hour of here that do hybrids, and Kestrel is one of them. If we moved, I'd be starting from scratch somewhere I don't know anyone. I'd rather fix the money than the postcode.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would the motorbike bring in?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: About eighteen hundred. That's more than I've ever had saved at once, which says a lot. I'd put it straight into a separate account so I can't touch it.

say: AI tools are **handy, not magic**, and the sellers oversold them.
I'd still use the assistant for **wiring diagrams** every day.
think: Being **the AI guy** at Kestrel matters less if the tools stay limited.
I'm an average mechanic on **below-average pay** with three weeks saved.
do: Keep using the assistant to save **twenty minutes** a job.
Ask Priyesh for a **raise** based on hybrid work.
Sell the unused **motorbike** and bank about eighteen hundred.
feel: **Flat** and a bit stuck, though not scared.
S0.quote: If AI stays a bit useful and nothing more, I'm just an average mechanic on below-average pay with three weeks of rent in the bank.
fieldNote: Aaron's **edge** at work comes from AI, so a plateau shrinks it.
His real pressure is **low pay** and thin savings, not job loss.
He'd rather **fix the money** than move, given few hybrid garages nearby.

steps.text: Ask Priyesh for a raise based on the hybrid work
Keep running fault logs through the AI assistant each morning
Sell the motorbike and bank the eighteen hundred separately

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Now that's the one I'd actually bet on. And I'd want to be on the right side of it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is good if the gains get shared, and bad if the bosses pocket it. I'd be telling the other lads at Kestrel to learn the tools now, not later. Online I'd be arguing for training money and a shorter week, not job cuts.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: For me it's mostly upside, at least at first. Booking, quotes, parts ordering and fault-finding all get faster, and I'm already doing that. The risk is Priyesh realising two mechanics with good AI can do the work of three.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask Priyesh to let me set up the AI booking and quoting system properly, and to pay me something for running it. I'd do an online course on battery and inverter repair. And I'd join the union, because if the job changes this much, someone needs to argue about how.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Mostly excited, with a nervous edge. Like the first time I drove a car I'd rebuilt.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who at Kestrel would you worry about?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Phil, who's been there twenty years and still writes his notes on the back of the job sheet. He's a better hands-on mechanic than me, honestly. But in this picture the one who reads the screen wins, and Phil won't.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What if Priyesh says no to paying you extra?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Then I'd still do it, because it makes me harder to let go. But I'd start looking at the bigger hybrid specialists in the city as a backup. I don't want to be the guy who built the system that replaced my workmate Phil and got nothing for it.

say: AI is good if **gains are shared** and bad if bosses pocket them.
Mechanics should push for **training money** and a shorter week, not cuts.
think: Booking, quotes and fault-finding getting faster is **mostly upside** for me.
Two mechanics with AI could do **the work of three**.
do: Offer to run Kestrel's **AI booking** and quoting, for extra pay.
Take an online **battery and inverter** repair course.
Join the **union** to have a say in how the job changes.
S1.quote: I don't want to be the guy who built the system that replaced my workmate Phil and got nothing for it.
fieldNote: Aaron sees Steady Disruption as **upside**, while naming the staffing risk.
His **progressive** views shape the deal he wants: shared gains, shorter week.
He worries for **Phil**, an older colleague who won't use screens.

steps.text: Set up and run Kestrel's AI booking and quoting system
Take an online battery and inverter repair course
Join the union and raise how AI changes the job
Look at city hybrid specialists as a backup

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Oof. Two years. Even I'm not that keen.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we need a plan from government before 2028, not after, with basic income or wage support. I'd be posting about it, and I'd be in every union chat. People think mechanics are safe, but the thinking half of the job is gone in this picture.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, my AI skills buy me maybe two years of being useful, running the systems at Kestrel. After 2028 the AI won't need me to check its answers. Then I'm just hands until about 2031, and after that robots do the hands too.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Right now I'd sell the motorbike, cut everything, and get the eighteen hundred into savings. I'd try to become the person who installs and fixes the robots and AI kit in garages, since that work comes first. In the first year after it arrives I'd chase any job maintaining the new machines, even if it means moving to the city.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, a real tight feeling. Being early on AI doesn't help much if everyone catches up in two years.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say to Sam that night?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell Sam we can't plan on my wage for long, and that we should look at where his bus job might go too. Then I'd probably open the laptop and start looking up robot technician courses at midnight, because that's how I cope.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Does the three-year gap before robots help you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Yes, more than most, because those three years are when garages are buying and setting up robots. Someone has to bolt them in, fix them, and keep them running. If I'm that someone, I might still have a job after 2031.

say: Government needs a **plan before 2028**, with income support.
The **thinking half** of mechanic work is gone in this picture.
think: My AI skills buy about **two years** running systems at Kestrel.
After **2031** robots do the hands too.
do: Sell the motorbike and **cut everything** to build savings.
Aim to become the person who **installs robots** in garages.
Chase **machine maintenance** jobs, even if it means moving city.
feel: Being early on AI helps **less than hoped**.
S2.quote: Being early on AI doesn't help much if everyone catches up in two years.
fieldNote: Aaron uses the **three-year gap** as a window to become a robot technician.
Even his **adaptability** feels thin against two years.
He worries about **Sam's** bus job too, not just his own.

steps.text: Sell the motorbike and bank the money straight away
Enrol on a robot technician course this year
Move to the city for machine maintenance work if needed
Push for wage support through union chats and posts

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years. That's enough time to actually do something clever.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is the moment to set up proper training, with garages, colleges and unions together. I'd be pushing for a co-op model where mechanics own a share of the robot gear.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, AGI in 2031 and robots in 2034 means I've got about seven years of hands-on work. If I spend the first three becoming a robot and AI technician, I'm one of the people who keeps the new kit running.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd do the battery and inverter course this year, then a robotics maintenance certificate the year after. I'd keep Kestrel as my day job and do evening work setting up AI booking systems for other small garages. I'd save the side money, not spend it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, but in a way that gets me out of bed. I like a deadline.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you charge other garages for setting up AI booking?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Maybe three hundred a garage, plus a small monthly fee for keeping it running. There are six or seven small garages within twenty miles. If half of them say yes, that's my emergency fund sorted in a year.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You mentioned a co-op. Would you really put money into that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If there was one, yes, even fifty a month. I'd rather own a slice of the robot than be replaced by the robot. But I haven't got the money to start one myself.

say: Garages, colleges and **unions** should set up training together now.
Mechanics should **own a share** of the robot gear through co-ops.
think: AGI in **2031** and robots in **2034** leave about seven years of hands-on work.
Spending three years retraining makes me the one who **keeps kit running**.
do: Take the **inverter course** this year and a robotics certificate next.
Set up **AI booking** for other small garages in the evenings.
Save all the **side money** for an emergency fund.
S3.quote: I'd rather own a slice of the robot than be replaced by the robot.
fieldNote: Five years lets Aaron plan a **two-step** retraining path.
His **side business** idea is concrete: three hundred a garage plus a fee.
The **co-op** idea comes from his progressive views but he can't fund it.

steps.text: Finish the battery and inverter course this year
Charge local garages three hundred to set up AI booking
Save all side earnings into an emergency fund
Put fifty a month into a mechanics' co-op if one forms

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ten years. That's comfortable. I'd be thirty-seven when the thinking side goes.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we have no excuse not to get this right. A decade is enough time to retrain every mechanic in the country if governments want to.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, ten years is my best case. I could build a real side business setting up AI for garages, get properly qualified on robots, and still be young enough for a third act after 2039.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd start the AI setup side work this year, slowly. I'd keep Kestrel full-time and do one course a year. I'd save enough to stop living month to month, which I've never managed.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Pretty calm about the change itself, uneasy about the money in between. Low pay doesn't go away just because the future looks better.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you need to stop living month to month?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Three months of rent, so about two and a half thousand. With the motorbike sale and side work, maybe eighteen months. That's the number I'd stick on the fridge.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Does the ten years change any plans with Sam?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: We've talked about buying somewhere. With ten years, I'd say let's save for a deposit and stop pretending we'll do it next year. With two, I'd keep renting and keep my options open.

There's **no excuse** not to get this right.
think: Ten years is my **best case** for building a side business.
I'd still be young enough for a **third act** after 2039.

Keep **Kestrel full-time** and do one course a year.
Save **three months' rent**, about two and a half thousand.

S4.quote: Low pay doesn't go away just because the future looks better.

He sets a clear **savings target** of two and a half thousand.
Time lets him and Sam consider **buying a home**.

steps.text: Start setting up AI systems for garages on the side

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The two-year one. I'm good with AI, but two years means everyone catches up and the robots come before I've saved anything. What would help is cheap, fast courses on robot maintenance and some income support while I do them.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Maybe about who owns the kit. Mechanics who know AI aren't scared of the tools; we're scared of not owning any of them. A share in the tools would change everything for people like me.

headlineQuote: Mechanics who know AI aren't scared of the tools; we're scared of not owning any of them.
portrait: Aaron, 27, works on **hybrids** at an industrial-estate garage and uses AI every day.
He has about **three weeks** of rent saved and below-average pay for his skills.
He sees Steady Disruption as **upside** but fears two mechanics with AI replacing three.
He'd use any warning time to become a **robot technician** and sell AI setup to garages.
He wants mechanics to **own a share** of the new tools, through co-ops or unions.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028**, because everyone catches up before he has any savings.
